Conductivity

Boltzmann Transport Equation (BTE)

QTrans calculates electrical conductivity and carrier mobility using the linearized Boltzmann transport equation (BTE) [3]. The equations below describe a spatially homogeneous system in a weak, static electric field, with phonons in thermal equilibrium and electron-phonon scattering as the collision mechanism.

We define the linear response of the electron distribution as

\[\partial_{E_\beta} f_{\nu\mathbf{k}} \equiv \left.\frac{\partial f_{\nu\mathbf{k}}}{\partial E_\beta} \right|_{\mathbf{E}=\mathbf{0}},\]

where \(\nu\) is the electron band index, \(\mathbf{k}\) is the electron wave vector, and \(\beta\) labels a Cartesian direction. Throughout this page, \(e>0\) is the elementary charge, so the electron charge is \(-e\). The equilibrium electron and phonon occupations are denoted by \(f^0_{\nu\mathbf{k}}\) and \(n^0_{\mathbf{q}b}\), respectively, where \(b\) is the phonon branch index.

The linearized BTE can be written as

\[\partial_{E_\beta} f_{\nu\mathbf{k}} = e\tau_{\nu\mathbf{k}}v_{\nu\mathbf{k}\beta} \frac{\partial f^0_{\nu\mathbf{k}}}{\partial\varepsilon_{\nu\mathbf{k}}} + \tau_{\nu\mathbf{k}}\sum_{\mu b} \int_{\mathrm{BZ}}\frac{d^3q}{\Omega_{\mathrm{BZ}}} K_{\nu\mathbf{k},\mu\mathbf{k+q}}^{b} \partial_{E_\beta} f_{\mu\mathbf{k+q}},\]

where \(\varepsilon_{\nu\mathbf{k}}\) is the electron energy, \(v_{\nu\mathbf{k}\beta}\) is the corresponding group velocity component, and \(\Omega_{\mathrm{BZ}}\) is the Brillouin-zone volume. The total relaxation time \(\tau_{\nu\mathbf{k}}\) is defined by

\[\begin{split}\tau_{\nu\mathbf{k}}^{-1} ={}& \frac{2\pi}{\hbar}\sum_{\mu b} \int_{\mathrm{BZ}}\frac{d^3q}{\Omega_{\mathrm{BZ}}} |g_{\mu\nu b}(\mathbf{k},\mathbf{q})|^2 \\ &\times\Big[ (n^0_{\mathbf{q}b}+1-f^0_{\mu\mathbf{k+q}}) \delta(\varepsilon_{\nu\mathbf{k}}-\varepsilon_{\mu\mathbf{k+q}} -\hbar\omega_{\mathbf{q}b}) \\ &\qquad+ (n^0_{\mathbf{q}b}+f^0_{\mu\mathbf{k+q}}) \delta(\varepsilon_{\nu\mathbf{k}}-\varepsilon_{\mu\mathbf{k+q}} +\hbar\omega_{\mathbf{q}b})\Big].\end{split}\]

Here, \(g_{\mu\nu b}(\mathbf{k},\mathbf{q})\) is the electron–phonon coupling matrix element, and \(\omega_{\mathbf{q}b}\) is the phonon angular frequency. The terms with \(-\hbar\omega_{\mathbf{q}b}\) and \(+\hbar\omega_{\mathbf{q}b}\) in the delta functions describe phonon emission and absorption, respectively. This expression is summed over all final electronic states and phonon modes; it is a total rate for the initial state \(\nu\mathbf{k}\), rather than a rate for a single transition.

The scattering-in kernel in the linearized BTE is

\[\begin{split}K_{\nu\mathbf{k},\mu\mathbf{k+q}}^{b} ={}& \frac{2\pi}{\hbar}|g_{\mu\nu b}(\mathbf{k},\mathbf{q})|^2 \\ &\times\Big[ (n^0_{\mathbf{q}b}+1-f^0_{\nu\mathbf{k}}) \delta(\varepsilon_{\nu\mathbf{k}}-\varepsilon_{\mu\mathbf{k+q}} +\hbar\omega_{\mathbf{q}b}) \\ &\qquad+ (n^0_{\mathbf{q}b}+f^0_{\nu\mathbf{k}}) \delta(\varepsilon_{\nu\mathbf{k}}-\varepsilon_{\mu\mathbf{k+q}} -\hbar\omega_{\mathbf{q}b})\Big].\end{split}\]

Unlike the expression for \(\tau_{\nu\mathbf{k}}^{-1}\), this kernel contains the equilibrium occupation of the initial state \(f^0_{\nu\mathbf{k}}\). It couples the distribution response at \(\mu\mathbf{k+q}\) to that at \(\nu\mathbf{k}\).

Electrical Conductivity and Mobility

The electrical conductivity tensor relates the induced current density to the applied field, \(j_\alpha=\sum_\beta\sigma_{\alpha\beta}E_\beta\):

\[\sigma_{\alpha\beta} = -\frac{e}{V_{\mathrm{uc}}}\sum_\nu \int_{\mathrm{BZ}}\frac{d^3k}{\Omega_{\mathrm{BZ}}} v_{\nu\mathbf{k}\alpha}\partial_{E_\beta}f_{\nu\mathbf{k}},\]

where \(V_{\mathrm{uc}}\) is the unit-cell volume. For a single carrier type in a semiconductor, the mobility tensor is obtained from its contribution to the conductivity:

\[\mu_{\alpha\beta}=\frac{\sigma_{\alpha\beta}}{e n_c},\]

where \(n_c>0\) is the carrier number density per unit volume. Electron and hole mobilities use their respective conductivity contributions and densities.

QTrans provides two methods for solving the BTE.

Self-Energy Relaxation Time Approximation (ERTA)

The self-energy relaxation time approximation, called ERTA in QTrans and also commonly abbreviated as SERTA, neglects the scattering-in term on the right-hand side of the linearized BTE. The distribution response is then

\[[\partial_{E_\beta}f_{\nu\mathbf{k}}]^{\mathrm{ERTA}} = e\tau_{\nu\mathbf{k}}v_{\nu\mathbf{k}\beta} \frac{\partial f^0_{\nu\mathbf{k}}}{\partial\varepsilon_{\nu\mathbf{k}}},\]

which gives

\[\sigma_{\alpha\beta}^{\mathrm{ERTA}} = \frac{e^2}{V_{\mathrm{uc}}}\sum_\nu \int_{\mathrm{BZ}}\frac{d^3k}{\Omega_{\mathrm{BZ}}} \left(-\frac{\partial f^0_{\nu\mathbf{k}}} {\partial\varepsilon_{\nu\mathbf{k}}}\right) v_{\nu\mathbf{k}\alpha}v_{\nu\mathbf{k}\beta}\tau_{\nu\mathbf{k}}.\]

Iterative Boltzmann Transport Equation (IBTE)

The iterative method retains the scattering-in term. Starting from the ERTA solution,

\[[\partial_{E_\beta}f_{\nu\mathbf{k}}]^{(0)} = [\partial_{E_\beta}f_{\nu\mathbf{k}}]^{\mathrm{ERTA}},\]

successive approximations are obtained from

\[[\partial_{E_\beta}f_{\nu\mathbf{k}}]^{(i+1)} = [\partial_{E_\beta}f_{\nu\mathbf{k}}]^{(0)} + \tau_{\nu\mathbf{k}}\sum_{\mu b} \int_{\mathrm{BZ}}\frac{d^3q}{\Omega_{\mathrm{BZ}}} K_{\nu\mathbf{k},\mu\mathbf{k+q}}^{b} [\partial_{E_\beta}f_{\mu\mathbf{k+q}}]^{(i)}.\]

The converged distribution response is used to evaluate the conductivity and, for a specified carrier density, the mobility.

Note

The equations above are written for one spin channel, or for a band index that explicitly includes all spin states. If a spin-degenerate system is represented using only one copy of each band, its total conductivity includes an additional factor of two. No extra factor is needed when spin states are counted explicitly. The carrier density used for mobility must follow the same spin-counting convention. QTrans includes the appropriate spin factor in its transport calculations.
